history.title: Find What It Is Really About

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Here is a skill that shows up on many reading tasks: figuring out the main point a text makes.

1. Read **The Suitcase Test** — it gives you a trick you can use forever.
2. Learn the words in the **Glossary**, then win the **Word Scramble** and the **Crossword**.
3. Keep the **Main Idea Moves** chart open while you work.
4. Practice on **Which Detail Does Not Belong?**
5. Take the quiz — it uses short paragraphs, so read each one twice.
6. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write your own main-idea statements.
7. Read **Reading Questions** if you are wondering how this works on videos, or what to do when you disagree with an author.
8. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Suitcase Test** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
9. Finish with **Design Challenge: A Main-Idea Poster for Younger Readers** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

Watch out for the most common trap: the topic is not the main idea. "Dogs" is a topic. "Dogs can be trained to detect illness" is a main idea. 🧳

Picture panels: Topic and main idea; Supporting details; Food-crop context; Read and check. Pictures support the lesson text and do not replace decoding or evidence from narration. Key lesson word-part examples have native editable labels; other schematic marks illustrate organization. Read sort statements in their supplied context. Educator review is pending.

history.title: The Suitcase Test
history.data:
## The Suitcase Test

Imagine you are packing a suitcase for a trip. The suitcase is the **main idea** — the one big container. The clothes you pack inside are the **supporting details**. Everything that goes in has to belong to that trip.

When you read a paragraph, you are doing the same job in reverse. You look at what is packed and figure out what suitcase it all came from.

Here is a paragraph:

> Honeybees do far more than make honey. As they move from flower to flower, pollen sticks to their bodies and travels with them, which lets plants make seeds. Many fruit and nut crops benefit from insect pollination. Farmers of almonds, apples, and blueberries even rent beehives during flowering season.

What is it about? A first instinct is "bees" — but that is only the **topic**, the one-word subject. The main idea is a full thought: *honeybees are important to our food supply because they pollinate crops.*

That is the difference students miss most. The topic can be a word or short phrase. The main idea is a sentence that says something ABOUT the topic.

Notice how the details worked. Pollen sticking to bees, food crops benefiting from pollination, farmers renting hives — each one supports the same claim. That is your test: if a detail does not support the main idea, it may be background or less relevant to this particular point.

Sometimes the main idea is stated right in the text, often in the first or last sentence. That is the easy version. Other times it is **implied** — never written down anywhere, and you have to build it yourself from the details. Both count. Both are findable.

A quick method that works: read the whole paragraph, then cover it and ask yourself, "If I could only say one sentence about this, what would it be?" Treat that sentence as a first draft, then check it against the important details.

One warning. A detail can be true, interesting, and still not be the main idea. "Bees have five eyes" is a fact, and it is fascinating, but a paragraph about pollination is not really about bee eyes. Interesting and important are different things — and telling them apart is most of what good reading is.

The suitcase is an analogy. Real paragraphs can include examples, qualifications and background. Focus on the important information, and allow more than one accurate wording of a main idea. You may keep the text visible, annotate, write or use AAC instead of covering it and speaking.

data.title: Remember the Suitcase Test
data.instructions: Each card locks in a move from The Suitcase Test. Study the example aid, make it yours, and tell how it helps you find what a text is really about.
data.sourceExcerpt: The suitcase is the main idea. The clothes you pack inside are the supporting details. The topic can be a word or short phrase. The main idea is a sentence that says something about the topic. Read the whole paragraph, then cover it and ask, 'If I could only say one sentence about this, what would it be?' Interesting and important are different things.

cards.target: Topic is a word; main idea is a sentence; details are what is packed inside
essentialFacts: The topic is what a text is about in a word or phrase.
The main idea is a full sentence that says something about the topic.
Supporting details are the pieces that belong inside that one idea.
cards.aiExample: The topic is the luggage tag (one word: 'Bees'). The main idea is the suitcase (a sentence: 'Bees matter to our food supply'). The details are the clothes packed inside, and every one must belong to the trip.
cards.mapping: Tag, suitcase, clothes: three sizes for three ideas. The tag is tiny like a topic word; the suitcase holds everything like the main idea; the clothes are the details that must fit.
cards.scaffoldStarter: The topic is the ____ (a word). The main idea is the ____ (a sentence). The details are the ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick your own container: a backpack, a lunchbox, a toy bin.
Match a label, the container, and the things inside to topic, main idea, and details.
Test it on the bee paragraph.
coachPrompts: In your analogy, what happens to a detail that does not belong to the trip?
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your analogy show that a topic is not the same as a main idea?

hookFact.text: 'Dogs' is a topic. 'Dogs can be trained to detect illness' is a main idea.

cards.target: The cover test: read, cover, say one sentence, check the details
essentialFacts: Cover it and ask: if I could only say one sentence about this, what would it be?
Check your sentence against the important details. A mismatch may mean revising your idea or recognizing background information.
cards.aiExample: Read. Cover. Say. Check. Four beats, four hand motions: eyes on the page, hand over the page, hand to your mouth, finger down the details.
cards.mapping: The four beats are the four steps in order, and the motions make the order physical so you do not skip 'check,' which is the step most people forget.
scaffoldSteps: Write the four steps as single words.
Run the test on one paragraph today.
coachPrompts: What would happen if you said your sentence before covering the page?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own four-beat version with motions.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your sequence keep you from stopping at the first sentence?

hookFact.text: After covering the paragraph, draft a main idea and check it against the important details.

cards.target: Interesting is not the same as important
essentialFacts: A detail can be true and fascinating and still not be the main idea.
'Bees have five eyes' is interesting, but a paragraph about pollination is not about bee eyes.
Ask whether the detail helps prove the main idea; if not, it does not belong in the suitcase.
cards.aiExample: Cool is not the same as key; does it prove the point to me?
cards.mapping: The first line names the trap (cool details feel key), and the second line is the test question from the reading, so the rhyme carries the fix along with the warning.
cards.scaffoldStarter: ____ is not the same as ____; does it ____?
scaffoldSteps: Choose two words for interesting and important that rhyme or bounce.
Try it on the five-eyes detail.
coachPrompts: Does your rhyme tell you what to DO with a cool detail, not just that it is a trap?
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your rhyme help you decide which details go in the suitcase?

hookFact.text: Telling interesting from important is most of what good reading is.

history.title: Find the Big Point

questions.question: What is the difference between a topic and a main idea?
options: A topic is always longer and more detailed than a main idea
A topic always appears in the very first sentence of a text
There is no real difference between the two terms
A topic is a word or phrase; a main idea is a full sentence about that topic
questions.correctAnswer: A topic is a word or phrase; a main idea is a full sentence about that topic

questions.question: Read: 'Sea otters eat sea urchins. Urchins eat kelp. Where otters were hunted out, urchins multiplied and kelp forests vanished. Where otters returned, kelp grew back.' What is the main idea?
options: Sea otters protect kelp forests by keeping urchin numbers down
Sea urchins eat kelp that grows along the rocky ocean floor
Sea otters were once hunted along the coast until they nearly vanished
Kelp forests are found in cold ocean water near the coast
questions.correctAnswer: Sea otters protect kelp forests by keeping urchin numbers down

questions.question: A main idea that is never written in the text is called what?
options: Stated
Implied
Irrelevant
Summarized

questions.question: You picked a main idea, but an important detail does not fit. What is the best next step?
options: The author made a mistake
That detail should be ignored completely
Your main idea may be too narrow — reconsider it
The paragraph has two topics and cannot be summarized
questions.correctAnswer: Your main idea may be too narrow — reconsider it

questions.question: Which of these is a MAIN IDEA rather than a topic?
options: Volcanoes can create new land over time
Volcanoes and the lava inside them
The lava and ash a volcano produces
The eruption of Mount St. Helens
questions.correctAnswer: Volcanoes can create new land over time

questions.question: Read this invented classroom example: 'The library opened a quiet corner. It added soft seats, dimmer lamps and sound-absorbing panels. Readers now have a place away from the busy entrance.' Write the main idea in one sentence.
questions.expectedAnswer: The library created a quieter, more comfortable place to read. Accept an equivalent statement that covers the changes and their purpose.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a detail being INTERESTING and a detail being IMPORTANT to the main idea. Use an example.
questions.expectedAnswer: An interesting detail catches attention but may not help prove the point. For example, 'bees have five eyes' is interesting, but in a paragraph about bees and our food supply it does not support the main idea, so it is not important there.

reflections.text: What is the main idea of the last thing you read outside of school?
Which is harder for you: finding a stated main idea or an implied one? Why?

history.meta: 5 MCQ + 2 short answer • real paragraphs to analyze

items.text: The topic of this text is ____.
One detail that supports this is ____.
Another detail that supports this is ____.
The detail about ____ is interesting, but it does not support the main idea because ____.
I think the main idea is stated / implied because ____.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Strong Reader |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main idea | Gives a topic word | A sentence, but too narrow or too broad | A sentence that covers the whole text exactly |
| Evidence | No details cited | One supporting detail | Two or more details quoted or paraphrased accurately |
| Judgment | Treats all details equally | Notices one off-topic detail | Explains WHY a detail does or does not support the idea |

data.question: Can a paragraph have more than one main idea? 🤔
data.answer: A paragraph often builds one main point. Some texts develop more than one. Choose a statement that fits the part you are reading.

data.question: Is the first sentence always the main idea?
data.answer: No. A writer may state it later or leave you to work it out. Check the details before choosing the first line.

data.question: What is the difference between a main idea and a summary? 📝
data.answer: The main idea names a key point. A summary also gives the most important details in a short account.

data.question: Why do tests love this skill so much?
data.answer: It helps you connect details and understand a text. You will also use other skills, such as working out new words or comparing ideas.

data.question: What if I disagree with the author's main idea?
data.answer: You can disagree. First explain the point fairly. Then use reasons and evidence to show why you disagree.

data.question: Does this work on videos and podcasts too? 🎧
data.answer: Yes. Pause, replay or use a transcript if it helps. Think about what the sounds and pictures add too.

history.meta: 4th-5th Grade • Design brief • teach the suitcase test to second graders

data.title: A Main-Idea Poster for Younger Readers
data.instructions: Design a one-page poster that teaches second graders how to find the main idea of a paragraph. Use a real paragraph, show the suitcase test working, and check that every detail on your poster belongs.
data.fitReason: Teaching a skill is the strongest test of having it. A poster for younger readers makes students choose a clear paragraph, apply the cover test in public, and prove the topic-versus-idea difference.

brief.context: The second-grade teacher down the hall has asked your class for posters her students can use during reading time. Her students can read short paragraphs but often answer 'What is it about?' with one word.
brief.drivingQuestion: How can one poster show a second grader the difference between a topic and a main idea, and walk them through finding the main idea of a real paragraph?
brief.seedDirection: Pick the paragraph first. If your example paragraph does not have one clear suitcase, no design will save the poster.
lockedLessonFacts: The topic is a word or phrase; the main idea is a sentence that says something about the topic.
Supporting details are the pieces that help prove the main idea.
The main idea can be stated in the text or implied, and both are findable.
The cover test: read the whole paragraph, cover it, say one sentence, check it against the details.
A detail can be interesting and still not be important to the main idea.
openQuestions: What paragraph is short enough and clear enough for a second grader?
How many words can a second grader read on a poster before they stop?
How do we show 'covering' the paragraph on paper?
Which detail on the poster is there because it is cool, not because it helps?
stakeholders: Their teacher, who has to explain it once
The librarian who may hang it
criteria: Shows a real paragraph of 4 to 6 sentences with its topic (a word) and main idea (a sentence) clearly labeled
Shows the four steps of the cover test in order
Every word on the poster is one a second grader can read or a picture explains
Includes one 'cool but not important' detail and says why it does not belong
Uses at least three glossary words correctly
constraints: Under 80 words on the poster itself, not counting the example paragraph
Must be readable from three feet away
brief.deliverable: A finished one-page poster plus a five-sentence note to the second-grade teacher explaining how to use it and which detail is the trap.

parallelExample.context: A fifth grader made a poster teaching kindergartners to tie shoes.
parallelExample.move: She tried to include every tip she knew and the poster got crowded. She tested it on a kindergartner, watched where he got lost, cut the poster to four steps with one picture each, and it worked.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Same design lesson: the poster is for the reader, not the maker. Test it on the real audience and cut everything that does not help them do the skill.

supports.frameStarter: Our paragraph is about ____ (topic). Its main idea is ____. The steps we show are ____. The trap detail is ____ because ____.
frameChoices: A comic strip of a reader doing the four steps
A suitcase drawing with details packed inside and one left out
A before-and-after: one-word answer versus one-sentence answer
A fill-in poster where the second grader writes the main idea
coachPrompts: Test your poster on someone younger. Where did they stop?
Is your example paragraph's main idea stated or implied, and did you tell the reader which?
Which word on the poster would a second grader not know?

data.coachHint: Fewer words, one clear paragraph, four steps in order. If it looks empty to you, it probably looks right to a second grader.
data.sourceExcerpt: A quick method that works: read the whole paragraph, then cover it and ask yourself, 'If I could only say one sentence about this, what would it be?'
